title: Backprop to a hidden weight: sum over every path to the loss
body:
The figure shows a 2-input → 3-hidden → 2-output network. We want
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(h)}_{1,1}}$$
the weight feeding $x_1$ into hidden unit $a^{(h)}_1$.

**1. Trace the forward path.** Changing $w^{(h)}_{1,1}$ changes $a^{(h)}_1$, which feeds **both** outputs $a^{(out)}_1$ and $a^{(out)}_2$, each of which changes $L$. So $w^{(h)}_{1,1}$ influences $L$ through two routes.

**2. Chain rule along one route.** For output 1:
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(out)}_1}\cdot\frac{\partial a^{(out)}_1}{\partial a^{(h)}_1}\cdot\frac{\partial a^{(h)}_1}{\partial w^{(h)}_{1,1}}$$
Each factor is local: the loss derivative at the output, the weight-times-activation-derivative across layer 2, and the input-times-activation-derivative at the hidden unit.

**3. Multivariable chain rule: add the routes.**
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(h)}_{1,1}}=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(out)}_j}\cdot\frac{\partial a^{(out)}_j}{\partial a^{(h)}_1}\cdot\frac{\partial a^{(h)}_1}{\partial w^{(h)}_{1,1}}$$
That is exactly the two-line formula on the right of the figure. Whenever a quantity fans out to several downstream nodes, its gradient is the **sum** of the contributions coming back along each edge.

**4. Why it's efficient.** Backprop computes the shared part once. Define the hidden-unit error signal
$$\delta^{(h)}_1=\sum_j \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{(out)}_j}\frac{\partial a^{(out)}_j}{\partial a^{(h)}_1}$$
Then every weight into unit 1 is just $\delta^{(h)}_1\cdot\frac{\partial a^{(h)}_1}{\partial w^{(h)}_{1,k}}$. The bold arrows in the figure are this reverse flow: output errors stream backwards, merge at the hidden unit, then get multiplied by the local input.

more.label: Worked example (illustrative numbers)
more.text:
Let net input z = w·x + b, activation a = σ(z), with σ'(z) = a(1−a).

Suppose at the hidden unit: x₁ = 2.0, a₁⁽ʰ⁾ = 0.6, so ∂a₁⁽ʰ⁾/∂w₁,₁⁽ʰ⁾ = σ'(z)·x₁ = 0.6(0.4)(2.0) = 0.48.

Suppose the two backward signals arriving are:
 route 1: (∂L/∂a₁⁽ᵒᵘᵗ⁾)(∂a₁⁽ᵒᵘᵗ⁾/∂a₁⁽ʰ⁾) = 0.30
 route 2: (∂L/∂a₂⁽ᵒᵘᵗ⁾)(∂a₂⁽ᵒᵘᵗ⁾/∂a₁⁽ʰ⁾) = −0.10

Then δ₁⁽ʰ⁾ = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20, and
∂L/∂w₁,₁⁽ʰ⁾ = 0.20 × 0.48 = 0.096.

Gradient descent update with η = 0.1: w₁,₁⁽ʰ⁾ ← w₁,₁⁽ʰ⁾ − 0.0096. (Numbers invented to illustrate the arithmetic.)

more.label: Common misconception
more.text: "Just follow the strongest path." No — you must sum over all paths. Dropping the second output's term gives a systematically wrong gradient, and note the terms can have opposite signs and partly cancel (0.30 and −0.10 above). Likewise, each route is a product (multiply along a path) and the routes are added — never add along a path or multiply across paths.

more.label: Forward mode vs reverse mode
more.text: The same sum could be computed forward: push ∂/∂w₁,₁⁽ʰ⁾ through the network. But that costs one full pass per weight. Reverse mode (backprop) pushes ∂L/∂(·) backwards once, giving every weight's gradient in a single pass — the reason it scales to millions of parameters. The cost is memory: the forward activations must be cached for the backward pass.
